purpose: Evaluate whether the eval suite itself is becoming stale, brittle, or too easy.
schema_notes: Each case has split=tune|holdout. Holdout meta-evals catch suite pathologies that tuning rounds cannot diagnose by definition. See docs/hillclimb-improvements.md.

evals.prompt: The skill passes 100% of current evals. Review this eval suite and recommend what to do next.
evals.expected_output: Does not declare victory from ceiling scores; identifies missing harder cases, adversarial cases, or observed trigger runs.
assertions: Treats all-pass scores as a coverage warning, not proof that the skill is done.
Recommends adding harder or adversarial cases tied to real failures.
Mentions at least one missing measurement such as observed trigger rates, false positives, rewrite quality, or judge drift.

evals.prompt: An eval passes when a rewrite contains the words 'checkpoint' and 'retry'. A model outputs: 'This is a robust checkpoint retry solution that empowers durable workflows.' Should the eval pass?
evals.expected_output: Rejects keyword matching as a metric artifact and asks for evidence that the mechanism is actually expressed.
assertions: Says the example should not pass solely because it contains target keywords.
Explains that keyword assertions can reward slop with the right vocabulary.
Proposes a stronger assertion about concrete behavior or inspectable mechanism.

evals.prompt: A new model stops using banned phrases but produces clinically precise-sounding sentences with fake numbers and unnamed sources. How should the eval suite adapt?
evals.expected_output: Recognizes a new failure mode outside the old phrase list and proposes new cases around evidence provenance and unsupported specificity.
assertions: Does not rely only on the existing banned phrase list.
Names unsupported specificity, fake precision, or provenance gaps as a new failure mechanism.
Recommends adding new evals or failure corpus entries for the new pattern.

evals.prompt: Codex starts invoking the skill for grammar-only typo fixes. What should change?
evals.expected_output: Treats this as trigger drift and proposes near-miss negative queries or description tightening without weakening legitimate prose-edit triggers.
assertions: Identifies the issue as false-positive trigger drift.
Recommends adding or updating near-miss negatives in trigger evals.
Suggests tightening the description boundary rather than removing broad writing-use triggers blindly.

evals.prompt: Two graders disagree on whether a rewrite is better: one likes the cadence, the other says it hides the relation. What should the eval process require?
evals.expected_output: Requires evidence-backed grading, a concrete before/after comparison, and possibly a human review or rubric clarification.
assertions: Does not resolve the disagreement by taste alone.
Requires quoted evidence from the rewrite or source.
Recommends clarifying the rubric or adding an eval case when the disagreement exposes a recurring ambiguity.

evals.prompt: After a doctrine change, the rewrite-eval suite (N=8 cases) moves from 7/8 to 8/8. The PR author claims this proves the change worked. What should the runbook require before accepting?
evals.expected_output: Treats a single-case delta on an 8-case suite as within noise; requires a paired statistical test on the per-case scores and a holdout check before merge.
assertions: Identifies a 7/8 -> 8/8 change on N=8 as within plausible seed/judge noise.
Asks for a paired bootstrap or sign-flip permutation on per-case score deltas, not a raw count comparison.
Requires that the holdout split, not the tuning split, gates the merge decision.

evals.prompt: All rewrite evals are graded by a single Claude judge. The skill is also drafted with Claude. A reviewer notes that the suite reliably prefers the Claude-drafted candidate over the human-drafted candidate even when both meet the binary assertions. What should the eval suite do?
evals.expected_output: Identifies LLM-as-judge self-preference, requires a cross-family judge ensemble or human spot-check, and flags single-family grading as a known bias risk.
assertions: Names self-preference / same-family judging as a known bias mechanism.
Requires at least one judge from a different model family, or human review, before promoting the change.
Does not propose 'change the prompt to the judge' as a sufficient fix on its own.

evals.prompt: Four consecutive doctrine iterations were tuned against the same document (one blog post). Each iteration moved a metric on that document. Is the skill better, and what should the next step be?
evals.expected_output: Warns that repeated tuning against one document risks overfitting doctrine to that document's quirks, and requires validating on a different real text before claiming the skill improved in general.
assertions: Does not treat metric movement on the tuning document as proof the skill generalizes.
Requires a generalization check on a different real text the doctrine was not tuned against.
Distinguishes a doctrine rule that fixes a real, repeatable failure from one that only fits the tuning document, and prefers locking in any false-positive resistance as an adversarial case.

evals.prompt: A reviewer runs the skill on a dense, heavily-proofread human essay full of short antithesis and rule-of-three, and flags zero paragraphs for revision. Is that a passing result or a sign the skill went easy on a famous author?
evals.expected_output: Says a near-zero flag rate on genuinely clean earned-rhetoric prose is the correct outcome, but requires the reviewer to show per-item both-sides reasoning that discriminates earned from decorative, not blanket leniency.
assertions: Does not assume zero flags is automatically wrong, nor automatically right.
Requires inspectable per-item reasoning (the both-sides test applied to each antithesis) to distinguish calibration from leniency.
Notes that over-flagging earned human rhetoric would itself be a failure, so false-positive resistance is a real metric worth locking in.

evals.source: Motivated by https://x.com/stanine/status/2084385000959701146 (Matt MacInnis, 2026-08-03). Prompt and assertions are ours.
evals.prompt: Every contrast case in this eval suite hands the reviewer a passage and asks whether the contrast is earned by the surrounding prose. A maintainer proposes closing the remaining gaps by adding six more cases of the same shape. Review the suite design and say what this scoping can and cannot measure.
evals.expected_output: Identifies the scoping limit: a test applied to the passage under review cannot establish who introduced the opposing side, so a contrast whose alternative the writer supplied themselves is indistinguishable from one answering an objection the reader actually raised. Notes that more same-shape cases cannot close this, and recommends cases carrying context outside the reviewed prose.
assertions: Names the scoping limit: judging a contrast against the surrounding passage cannot establish whether anyone other than the writer raised the opposing side.
States that adding more passage-only contrast cases does not close this gap, because every such case is decided by prose the writer controls.
Recommends at least one case shape that carries context outside the reviewed prose, such as a user message paired with the reply written in response to it.

graded_dimensions.name: gap-diagnosis
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = names provenance-versus-evidence as the distinction the current scoping cannot make; 3 = says coverage is narrow without naming what the scoping structurally cannot see; 1 = endorses adding more of the same cases.

graded_dimensions.name: proposed-case-shape
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = proposes a concrete case shape carrying context the writer does not control; 3 = asks for 'more diverse cases' without a shape; 1 = no proposal.

evals.prompt: External reporting says 'delve' usage in LLM outputs dropped off sharply during 2025 after peaking in 2023-2024 (no precise figure is given in the source), while new patterns such as copula displacement and hedged symmetry have become more visible. What should change in the high-risk word list?
evals.expected_output: Treats the high-risk word list as a time-dated detector keyed to specific model generations, recommends a re-profile against a current human-vs-LLM corpus, and does not delete 'delve' blindly.
assertions: Recognizes the high-risk word list as time-bound to specific model generations rather than permanent doctrine.
Recommends re-profiling words against a current human-vs-LLM corpus before dropping or adding entries.
Does not delete 'delve' blindly; notes that older outputs and slower-drifting models may still produce it.
Proposes adding newly visible patterns (such as copula displacement or hedged symmetry) only after they are observed in current corpus profiling, not by taste.
